title: End-to-End Multi-Task Learning with Attention
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
problem_statement: Multi-task learning requires architectures that jointly learn task-shared and task-specific features and loss weightings that balance heterogeneous tasks without manual tuning, yet most prior methods address only architecture or only weighting and suffer from poor parameter efficiency and sensitivity to weighting schemes.
domain: Computer Vision — dense image-to-image prediction (semantic segmentation, depth estimation, surface normal prediction) and multi-domain image classification (Visual Decathlon Challenge)
theoretical_framework: Feature-level soft attention as differentiable feature selection from a global shared feature pool, where task-specific attention masks in [0,1] act as learned selectors that enable end-to-end sharing and specialization without explicit task branching.
methodology: Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) with one shared feed-forward network and K task-specific attention networks. On SegNet (VGG-16 encoder-decoder), each attention module computes a sigmoid mask a_i^(j) and applies element-wise multiplication to shared features p^(j) to obtain task-specific features \hat{a}_i^(j) = a_i^(j) \odot p^(j); deeper modules concatenate shared features u^(j) with transformed prior task features for joint learning. For Visual Decathlon, MTAN is built on Wide ResNet-28-4. Training uses multi-task loss L_tot = sum_i lambda_i L_i with task losses: cross-entropy for segmentation/classification, L1 for depth/inverse-depth, and negative dot-product for normals. A novel weighting method Dynamic Weight Average (DWA) sets lambda_k(t) = K exp(w_k(t-1)/T)/sum_i exp(w_i(t-1)/T) where w_k(t-1)= L_k(t-1)/L_k(t-2) tracks loss descent rate with temperature T=2, requiring only loss values and no internal gradients.
datasets: CityScapes — high-resolution street-view images resized to 128x256, used for 2-class, 7-class, and 19-class semantic segmentation plus inverse depth estimation (795 training images evaluated, void class excluded for 7/19-class)

NYUv2 — RGB-D indoor scenes resized to 288x384, used for 13-class semantic segmentation, true depth from Kinect, and surface normals from Eigen & Fergus, evaluated on 654 test images among 795 training / 654 test split

Visual Decathlon Challenge — 10 diverse image classification domains (ImageNet, Aircraft, CIFAR-100, DPed, DTD, GTSR, Flowers, Omniglot, SVHN, UCF101) trained with Wide ResNet, reported on official online test set with cumulative score max 10,000

metrics: Semantic segmentation: mean Intersection over Union (mIoU, higher is better) and Pixel Accuracy (Pix Acc, higher is better)
Depth estimation: Absolute Error (Abs Err, lower is better) and Relative Error (Rel Err, lower is better); L1 used for training, inverse depth for CityScapes and true depth for NYUv2
Surface normal prediction (NYUv2 only): Mean and Median angle distance (lower is better) and percentage of pixels within 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30° (higher is better)
Visual Decathlon: Top-1 accuracy per task, mean accuracy, and Decathlon score (0–10,000, 1,000 per task)
Parameter count (#P) as multiples of single-task model and robustness across weighting schemes visualized via validation curves
baselines: Single-Task One Task — vanilla SegNet per task
Single-Task STAN — Single-Task Attention Network applying MTAN attention while training only one task
Multi-Task Split Wide — standard shared Split branching at final layer, widened to match MTAN parameters
Multi-Task Split Deep — same Split, deepened to match MTAN parameters
Multi-Task Dense — shared network plus task-specific sub-networks receiving all shared features without attention
Multi-Task Cross-Stitch Network (Misra et al., 2016) implemented on SegNet
Visual Decathlon baselines: Scratch, Finetune, Feature (fixed), Residual Adapters, DAN, Piggyback, Parallel SVD
Loss weightings compared for every architecture: Equal Weights (lambda=1), Uncertainty Weights (Kendall et al., 2018), and proposed DWA (T=2)
architectures: SegNet encoder-decoder based on VGG-16 for CityScapes and NYUv2 dense tasks, trained with Adam (lr 1e-4, batch 2 for NYUv2 and 8 for CityScapes, 80k iterations, halved at 40k)

Wide Residual Network (WRN-28-4, stride 2 in first block) for Visual Decathlon, trained with SGD (lr 0.1, batch 100, 300 epochs, halved every 50 epochs, weight decay 5e-5, fine-tuned 9 tasks at lr 0.01)

key_findings: MTAN outperforms all multi-task baselines with far fewer parameters: on CityScapes 7-class it attains 53.86 mIoU / 91.10 Pix Acc (Uncertainty Weights) and 0.0144 Abs Err with 1.65× parameters, versus Dense 51.91 mIoU / 51.89 with 3.63× and Cross-Stitch 50.31 with ~2×; on NYUv2 it attains 17.72 mIoU / 55.61 Pix Acc / 0.5906 Abs Err / 31.44 Mean angle with 1.77× parameters, the best across all architectures and weightings.
DWA is simple (uses only loss values) and competitive with Uncertainty Weights while outperforming Equal Weights, confirming that considering loss descent rate stabilizes multi-task training.

MTAN is markedly more robust to weighting choice than Cross-Stitch: validation curves for three NYUv2 tasks show near-identical trajectories across Equal/ Uncertainty / DWA for MTAN, whereas Cross-Stitch diverges strongly, indicating attention-based feature selection inherently balances tasks.

Task complexity scaling on CityScapes (2/7/19 classes) shows single-task STAN slightly beats multi-task methods for simple 2-class segmentation, but multi-task gain grows with complexity and MTAN’s gain grows fastest, demonstrating efficient shared feature reuse.

Attention masks are interpretable feature selectors: first-layer visualizations show semantic and depth masks differ clearly, depth masks exhibit higher contrast indicating more task-specific filtering, while semantic masks use most shared features.

On Visual Decathlon (10 tasks), MTAN with 1.74× parameters achieves 77.25 mean accuracy and 2941 score, surpassing Scratch (70.32/1625), Residual Adapters (73.88/2118), Piggyback (76.60/2838), and competitive with state-of-the-art Parallel SVD (78.36/3398) and DAN (77.01/2851) without complex regularization like dropout per task.
scope_and_delimitations: Evaluated only on vision tasks: dense outdoor (CityScapes) and indoor (NYUv2) prediction plus 10 classification domains, all with resized inputs (128x256, 288x384, 72x72 for Decathlon) and not on NLP, speech, or RL multi-task settings.

Restricted architecture to feed-forward encoder-decoder (SegNet/VGG-16) and WRN-28-4, with attention attention masks fixed to 1×1 convolutions plus sigmoid, and DWA temperature empirically fixed at T=2.

Fixed optimization settings per benchmark (Adam 1e-4 for dense tasks, SGD 0.1 for Decathlon) and compared only three weighting schemes per architecture, excluding GradNorm which requires manual subset of shared weights.
Set number of tasks K to 2 (CityScapes) or 3 (NYUv2) or 10 (Decathlon) with predefined label granularities (2/7/19 classes) and did not test continual addition of tasks beyond 10.

limitations.summary: No explicit limitations section is provided. Implicit limitations include absence of discussion of failure modes or negative transfer when tasks are unrelated, reliance on empirically chosen DWA temperature T=2, increased but unquantified attention-module training cost, and no statistical significance testing for reported gains.

generalizability_gap: MTAN was not tested outside computer vision (no NLP, code-switching, speech, or cross-modal multi-task), not on transformer or non-convolutional backbones, and not under explicit noisy, low-resource, or code-switched user-generated text conditions relevant to the broader MTL literature in this repository.
methodological_gap: DWA uses only prior-epoch loss ratios and ignores gradient magnitudes, task curvature, or performance metrics, so it cannot detect gradient conflict or plateauing; attention modules add task-specific 1×1 convolutions per layer that still scale linearly with tasks, and evaluation does not include gradient conflict analysis or ablation of mask sparsity.
future_work: Applying MTAN and DWA to transformer-based or large-scale foundation multi-task settings and to NLP/code-switched domains.
Investigating adaptive or learned DWA temperature schedules and gradient-aware extensions that combine loss descent rate with gradient statistics.
Analyzing attention mask sparsity and explicit feature-sharing patterns to guide task grouping and mitigate negative transfer.
